3. Open a pull request here that adds a row to [Listed adapters](#listed-adapters), with the checklist below.
4. We review the signing and confirmation code, run the checks and look at the testnet transactions.
5. You are listed as Verified. Each new major version is reviewed again.

**Pull request checklist** (copy it into the PR description):

```markdown
- [ ] Adapter card in the package README
- [ ] Conformance checks pass in CI: <link to the run>
- [ ] Testnet paid job: <transaction hash>, confirmed by the client
- [ ] Testnet recovery drill: one job, one transfer: <transaction hash>
- [ ] The adapter never submits, sends or settles a payment itself
- [ ] No keys, signed payloads or job tokens in logs or telemetry
- [ ] Security contact: <email or URL>
```

## Listed adapters

| Adapter | Slot | Level | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Local key (`localKeySigner`) | Signer | Built-in | [payment-client](../../packages/payment-client/src/local-key-signer.ts) |
| x402 exact on Stellar (`x402-exact-stellar`) | Payment method | Built-in | [payment-client](../../packages/payment-client/src/x402-exact-stellar.ts) |

Planned, not built: Stellar Wallets Kit, passkey smart accounts, Eunomia, ERC-8196 policy wallets. See
[payment-client.md](../payment-client.md#strategies-signers-and-payment-methods).

## Not ready on our side yet

- The payment client is not on npm yet. Until it is, build your adapter as a package in a fork of this repo.
- The conformance checks don't test what a payment method signs. We check it by hand in review.
- Smart accounts (`C…`) can't pay through the built-in payment method yet. They need their own method.
- There is no conformance suite for native clients yet. Test against the example service and its drills.
- The web app doesn't show trust levels yet.

## Learn more

- [AI-readable version](README-AI.md)
- [Payment client design](../payment-client.md)
- [Provider Standard, in short](../standard/README.md), and its [client rules](../standard/README-AI.md#14-client-rules-agents-wallets-apps)
- [Payment client package](../../packages/payment-client/README.md)
- [Example service](../../examples/paid-service/README.md)


<!-- ===== docs/payment-client.md ===== -->

# Payment Client: design

> Status: **accepted** (2026-10-21). A proof of concept of the core, the local-key signer and a CLI is in
> [packages/payment-client](../packages/payment-client), and a minimal web page on the same core is in
> [apps/wallet](../apps/wallet) (2026-10-22). IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md §5.6 and principle 3 follow this design.

## Who it is for

- **Developers and their agents** in Claude Code, Codex or their own code. The agent finds and pays services
  on its own, inside a budget the human set.
- **Non-technical users** who open a web page, pick a service, fill in a form and pay, with no seed phrase,
  CLI or browser extension required.

The aim is a product people would use after the grant, not just a demo for the SOW: **a wallet for AI
agents, with spending rules set by a human**. It is the demand side of the Provider Standard.

## Fixed requirements

- Wallet separation: keys never touch discovery or provider code.
- Explicit approval of the service, price, recipient, asset, network and when the user is charged (`charge`).
- Spending controls: a per-payment cap and a rolling budget. A failed limit check blocks the payment.
- Challenge validation against the approved manifest (provider-standard.md [P4], [P7]).
- Durable journal before sending: job id, Job-Token and binding hash. Never re-sign the same job.
- Recovery through check-status and get-result only.
- On-chain settlement proof before showing "paid": the `transfer` event matches the approved payment
  (provider-standard.md [J16]).
- No custody: we never hold a user's key on a server (SOW out of scope, and a regulatory burden).

## Decision

### Shape: one core, two strategies, two surfaces

```
   Web app (everyone)              MCP server (agents)
   browse · form · approve ·       find · quote · pay · status ·
   budget · history · recover      result · budget
              │                            │
              └──────────┬─────────────────┘
                         ▼
             payment-client core (TypeScript, no UI)
   manifest → checkChallenge → pick method → policy + budget → approve → sign → journal → send → confirm
                │                                                           │
                ▼                                                           ▼
   PaymentMethod  (how a payment is made)                     Signer  (who holds the key)
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐                ┌──────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────┐
   │ x402 exact on Stellar (USDC) │                │ local key    │ Stellar Wallets  │ smart account:   │
   │ later: other schemes/assets  │                │ (dev, CI,    │ Kit: Freighter,  │ passkey owner +  │
   │ once the standard has them   │                │  allowance)  │ xBull, Lobstr, … │ scoped agent key │
   └──────────────────────────────┘                └──────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────┘
```

- **Core** (`packages/payment-client`): everything that has to be right for money to be safe. It has no UI and
  no key storage, and the same code runs in Node and the browser.
- **Signers** plug in behind one interface, so the core never sees how a key is held.
- **Payment methods** plug in behind another, so a new way to pay never touches the safety rules. See
  [Strategies](#strategies-signers-and-payment-methods).
- **Web app** (`apps/wallet`, static, no backend): the main UI for everyone, and what the D1 video shows. The
  minimal page is built (2026-10-22): a test wallet, the form from the schema, the approval screen, spending
  limits, recent payments and recovery, with the local-key signer.
  - Turns each service's `inputSchema` into a form, so any provider is usable with no frontend work.
  - Shows price, payee, verification badges and `charge` on one approval screen.
  - Budget settings, history with explorer links, and a "recover job" button.
- **MCP server** (`packages/payment-mcp`): a separate server with its own key, apart from the read-only search
  server. Inside the budget it pays without asking. Above the budget it asks for approval, through MCP
  elicitation or a link to the web app.

### Where keys live

| Key | Who holds it | Can do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owner key | The human: a passkey (Face ID / Touch ID) or Freighter | Anything: fund, set and revoke policies, approve large payments |
| Agent key | The MCP server or SDK, on the developer's machine | Only what the policy allows |
| — | Our servers | Nothing. There is no key on any server. |

The agent key is what lets an agent pay without a prompt, so how much damage it can do has to be limited:
- **Weeks 1–2: allowance wallet.** The agent key controls a separate `G…` account that the owner tops up with
  a small amount. The client enforces the policy off chain. The most it can lose is that account's balance.
- **Target: smart account.** The owner's passkey and the agent key are both signers on one Soroban smart
  account, whose `__check_auth` enforces the agent's policy on chain. Even a compromised agent machine can't
  spend beyond the policy. Contract accounts hold USDC without a trustline, which removes a step for
  non-technical users.

### Strategies: signers and payment methods

**Built 2026-10-22**, with the built-ins only (`packages/payment-client/src/strategies.ts`).

The core uses the Strategy pattern on two independent axes. Other Stellar wallets and payment infrastructure
can then be plugged in later without changing the core: ours, existing projects such as Eunomia or an
ERC-8196 wallet, or new ones. Any signer works with any method that supports it.

```ts
/** Who holds the key: the SEP-43 shape @x402/stellar signs with. */
interface Signer {
  address: string;                       // G… or C…
  signAuthEntry: SignAuthEntry;
  signTransaction?: SignTransaction;
  /** A policy wallet's remaining on-chain budget for `asset`, in base units. Undefined: no limit. */
  budget?(network: StellarNetwork, asset: string): Promise<string | undefined>;
}

/** How an x402 challenge entry is paid, and how that payment is proven. */
interface PaymentMethod {
  id: string;                            // "x402-exact-stellar", journaled with each payment
  matches(requirements: PaymentRequirements): boolean;
  createPayload(requirements: PaymentRequirements, signer: Signer): Promise<SignedPayload>;
  confirm(transaction: string, expected: ExpectedPayment): Promise<Confirmation>;
}
```

The built-ins are `localKeySigner(secret, network)` and `x402ExactStellar({ rpcUrl })`.
`new PaymentClient({ signer, methods })` uses `[x402ExactStellar()]` when `methods` is not given.

**The core keeps every safety step; adapters can't skip them.** For every signer and method:

1. `checkChallenge()`: the challenge equals the manifest's payment option [P4].
2. The first installed method whose `matches()` is true pays. If none matches, or `matches()` throws, the
   payment is refused before anything is signed.
3. The terms the user approves (network, asset, amount, payTo) come from the challenge entry, never from an
   adapter, so no adapter can change them.
4. The spending policy applies, and so does a policy wallet's `budget()`. A budget that is too low, can't be
   read, or isn't in base units blocks the payment (fail closed). Both run again inside `pay()`.
5. Approval, then journal `approved`.
6. `createPayload()` signs. Only one `pay()` per job runs at a time, so a slow wallet popup can't lead to a
   second signature. If the wallet does not sign, the core journals `refused`. Nothing was sent, so the user
   can try again.
7. Journal `sending` with the terms, the payer and the method id, and flush it. Only then send.
8. The method recorded in `sending` confirms the payment against the journaled terms. If that method is not
   installed, or it throws, the result is "not confirmed" with a reason, never "paid".

**Conformance checks** (`@stellar-agent-services/payment-client/conformance`). The core enforces the steps
above whatever is plugged in, so these checks cover what only an adapter can get right. They work with any
test framework.

| For | Checks |
| --- | --- |
| Signers: `signerConformance()` | Has a Stellar `G…` or `C…` address. Signs an auth entry as its own address. For a `G…` key, the signature verifies against it. `budget()`, if present, reports base units. |
| Payment methods: `paymentMethodConformance()` | Has a stable id. Matches its own entry, but not an unknown scheme, an unknown network or a malformed entry. Confirms a settled payment, but not the same transaction with another payee, amount, asset or payer. |

The built-ins pass them, and the test suite also checks that they fail broken adapters.

**Adapters and trust levels.** An adapter for another wallet or payment infrastructure lives in its own package
(`signer-<name>` or `method-<name>`). It depends on the core's types, and the core never depends on it. Users
see how far we vouch for each one:

| Level | Meaning | Shown as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Built-in | Ours, in this package: `localKeySigner`, `x402ExactStellar` | No label |
| Verified | Passes the conformance checks, and we reviewed it | A "verified" badge |
| Community | Anyone's adapter that we have not reviewed | A warning at setup |

A wallet's own security, such as how it stores its key, stays its own responsibility. The core guarantees only
that what leaves through it is what the user approved.

How to build, test and submit an adapter, and what we and the integrator each need, is in
[client-integration/README.md](client-integration/README.md) (for AI agents:
[README-AI.md](client-integration/README-AI.md)).

**Integrations, later.** None is built yet. Each will be its own package.

| Integration | Slot | Status and what to check first |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Stellar Wallets Kit](https://stellarwalletskit.dev): Freighter, xBull, Lobstr, Albedo, Hana, … | Signer | Week 1 spike: which wallets' `signAuthEntry` works with `@x402/stellar` |
| Passkey smart account (OpenZeppelin) | Signer, with `budget()` from its policy | Week 3 spike: a `C…` account paying through the facilitator |
| [Eunomia](https://github.com/eunomia-finance/eunomia) treasury | Signer with `budget()` if its treasury can authorize the SAC `transfer` that x402 `exact` uses; otherwise a payment method, which needs a Provider Standard change | Testnet only. Read its `packages/x402` first. |
| ERC-8196 policy wallet (a parallel project) | Signer with `budget()` | In development. Our policy and journal already use ERC-8196 field names. |
| Other x402 schemes (such as `upto`) or other assets | Payment method | Each needs a Provider Standard change and a provider that offers it |

### Policy (ERC-8196 field names plus Stellar extensions)

| Field | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `policyId`, `ownerAddress`, `agentAddress` | ERC-8196 | — |
| `agentId` | The agent's Stellar 8004 id, if it has one | unset |
| `allowedActions` | `["x402.pay"]` | — |
| `allowedContracts` / `blockedContracts` | The asset contract (USDC SAC) | USDC only |
| `maxValuePerTx`, `maxValuePerDay` | In the asset's base units, not a native value | 0.10 / 1.00 USDC |
| `validAfter`, `validUntil` | ERC-8196 | now / +30 days |
| `minVerificationScore` | ERC-8196, read through a risk-source interface once a Stellar ERC-8126 exists | unset |
| `stellar.asset` | The one asset the limits apply to | USDC |
| `stellar.payees` | `{ allow?, block? }` lists of `payTo` addresses, since the real payee is an argument of `transfer` | unset |
| `stellar.minProviderLevel` | The lowest `provider-standard-v1` conformance level a payee must have | unset (pilot) |
| `stellar.autoApproveUpTo` | Payments at or below this amount, and inside the limits, need no prompt | **0: approve every payment** |

`policyHash = sha256(JCS(policy))`. Every journal entry and every approval names the policy hash it ran under.
Out of the box, every payment asks for approval, which is what the SOW requires. Paying without a prompt is
something the owner turns on.

### Journal (ERC-8196 hash-chained audit trail)

- One entry per step: `intent`, `approved` or `refused` (with the policy rule that refused), `sending`,
  `settled` or `uncertain`, `recovered`, `result`.
- Each entry has `seq`, `previousHash`, `policyHash`, `jobId`, `service`, `baseUrl`, `bindingHash`, `amount`,
  `payTo`, the payment method and, when known, the transaction hash. `hash = sha256(JCS(entry))`.
- `sending` is written, and flushed to disk, **before** the paid request goes out. Recovery starts from the
  last `sending` with no `settled` or `result` after it, and never re-signs that job.
- Job tokens are secrets, so they are stored next to the journal, not in it. The journal can then be exported
  or anchored without exposing them.
- Storage is a file in Node (the `./node` entry point) and IndexedDB in the browser (`./browser`, written with
  strict durability). A journal has one writer, so the web app runs in one tab at a time. Anchoring a Merkle root
  on chain is later work.

### One payment, step by step

1. Fetch the manifest and validate it (the protocol package).
2. Build the job: `jobId`, `Job-Token` and binding hash. Journal `intent`.
3. Call create-job without paying and get the 402. `checkChallenge()` against the manifest, and pick the
   payment method that matches it. A violation, or no matching method, refuses.
4. Policy check, plus the wallet's own budget for a policy wallet. If either fails, journal `refused` and
   stop (fail closed). If the amount is above `autoApproveUpTo`, show the approval screen. `decline()` journals
   `refused` and never signs.
5. Journal `approved`, sign, then journal `sending` and send. A busy provider (`429` or `503`, spec §5.8) answers
   before it takes the payment: the client waits out `Retry-After` and sends the same signed request again, while
   the payment is still valid and for at most `busyWaitSeconds`. If the provider stays busy, it journals `failed`
   with `charged: false`. The unpaid request in step 3 is waited out the same way.
6. Get the job view. Confirm the USDC `transfer` on chain before showing "paid", then journal `settled`.
7. On `202`, or if the connection drops: check-status, then get-result, never paying again, at the pace the
   provider's `Retry-After` sets. A `409 request_in_progress` means the provider holds the payment and is still
   settling it: the client keeps polling, and hands the job back for `recover()` if settlement outlasts
   `followSeconds`. A job the provider marks `payment_uncertain` comes back at once: only the provider's
   reconciliation resolves it ([job-recovery.md](job-recovery.md#reconciliation)), so polling doesn't.

## Sprint plan

| Week | Build | Shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Core (policy, journal, x402 flow, recovery skeleton), local-key signer, a minimal approval page. Spike: Stellar Wallets Kit, listing the wallets whose `signAuthEntry` works with `@x402/stellar`. | The first paid testnet transaction; the D1 video of the approval screen |
| 2 | Web app v1: form from schema, approval, budget, history. MCP server: paying inside the budget, approval above it. | Developers and non-technical users can both run the flow |
| 3 | Recovery in both surfaces. Spike: a passkey smart account paying an x402 service through the facilitator. | The recovery demo |
| 4 | Pilot. If the spike passed, non-technical pilot users get passkey wallets. | Five user flows |

The smart account is the flagship, but no SOW deliverable depends on it: the allowance wallet and Freighter
cover the sprint whatever the spike shows.

## Risks and open points

- **Browser calls need CORS.** The web app calls providers straight from the browser. Provider Standard v1
  makes this a SHOULD ([J17]) and Provider Kit turns it on by default. A provider without CORS is reachable
  only through the MCP server or SDK.
- **Browser wallets:** whether each wallet's `signAuthEntry` output fits what `@x402/stellar` expects is
  unverified (Week 1 spike, through Stellar Wallets Kit). Freighter is the first to test. Fallback for the D1
  video: the local-key signer behind the same approval page.
- **Smart account x402 payments** are unverified (erc-compatibility.md, T5). We use an existing audited
  smart-account contract, such as OpenZeppelin's Stellar smart accounts, rather than writing our own. Building
  an ERC-8196 contract stays with the parallel project.
- **Moving money in and out** for non-technical users on mainnet: many exchanges can't send to a `C…` address.
  On testnet we pre-fund pilot wallets.
- **Principle 3** (IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md) now reads: the user approves each exact payment, or the payment
  fits a budget the user explicitly granted.

## Options considered

| Option | Why it was not chosen alone |
| --- | --- |
| Node library + CLI with an encrypted keystore | Fine for developers, unusable for non-technical users. It survives as the core plus the local-key signer. |
| Keyed MCP server with elicitation | Agents only. It survives as one of the two surfaces. |
| Browser page with Freighter | Needs an extension, and every payment needs a human, so agents can't act on their own. It survives as one signer, through Stellar Wallets Kit. |
| Payment methods as separate options (`createPayload`, `confirmPayment`, as in the first PoC) | Nothing tied a method's payload to its proof, so a new method could pair them wrongly. Replaced by `PaymentMethod` on 2026-10-22. |
| Hosted wallet that holds keys | Custody, which is out of scope and a regulatory burden. |


<!-- ===== packages/payment-client/README.md ===== -->

# @stellar-agent-services/payment-client

The buyer side: approval, spending policy, a hash-chained journal, payment and job recovery. The design is in
[docs/payment-client.md](../../docs/payment-client.md).

**Status: proof of concept.** The core flow works end to end on Stellar testnet with the built-in signer and
payment method, both in Node (the `stellar-pay` CLI) and in the browser (the minimal web page in
[apps/wallet](../../apps/wallet)). The MCP server, browser-wallet and passkey signers come later and reuse this core.

Signers and payment methods are strategies: the core keeps every safety step, and adapters for other wallets or
payment infrastructure plug in without changing it (docs/payment-client.md, "Strategies"). To build one, see
[docs/client-integration](../../docs/client-integration/README.md).

```ts
const client = new PaymentClient({
  signer: localKeySigner(secret, "stellar:testnet"), // or a wallet adapter
  methods: [x402ExactStellar()],                      // the default
  policy, journal, secrets,
});
```

The main entry point runs in Node and the browser. Journal storage depends on where it runs:

| Entry point | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `@stellar-agent-services/payment-client` | The core, the built-in signer and payment method |
| `…/node` | `fileJournalStorage`, `fileSecretStore`: files only the owner can read |
| `…/browser` | `indexedDbJournalStorage`, `indexedDbSecretStore`: IndexedDB with strict durability |
| `…/conformance` | The checks every adapter must pass |

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `src/client.ts` | `PaymentClient`: `quote()` (nothing signed), `pay()` (signs once), `decline()`, `recover()` (never pays) |
| `src/strategies.ts` | The `Signer` and `PaymentMethod` interfaces |
| `src/local-key-signer.ts` | The built-in signer: a secret key in this process |
| `src/x402-exact-stellar.ts` | The built-in payment method: x402 `exact` on Stellar, the only one Provider Standard v1 allows |
| `src/conformance.ts` | Checks that every signer and payment-method adapter must pass (`./conformance` entry point) |
| `src/policy.ts` | Spending policy with ERC-8196 field names; `checkPolicy()` fails closed |
| `src/journal.ts` | Append-only, hash-chained journal; job tokens kept apart in a `SecretStore` |
| `src/file-storage.ts` | Journal and job-token storage in files (`./node` entry point) |
| `src/browser-storage.ts` | Journal and job-token storage in IndexedDB (`./browser` entry point) |
| `src/manifest.ts` | Fetches and validates a provider manifest |
| `src/onchain.ts` | Confirms the settlement transaction on chain |
| `src/cli.ts` | `stellar-pay`, the PoC surface |

## Try it on testnet

```bash
npm install && npm run build

# A provider wallet (it only needs a USDC trustline) and a payer wallet with testnet USDC.
STELLAR_PAY_HOME=~/.stellar-pay-provider npx stellar-pay wallet create
STELLAR_PAY_HOME=~/.stellar-pay-provider npx stellar-pay wallet fund --usdc 0
npx stellar-pay wallet create
npx stellar-pay wallet fund --usdc 2          # buys testnet USDC on the testnet DEX

# The sample provider, paid to the provider wallet's address.
PAY_TO=G... node examples/paid-service/dist/server.js

# Pay, with an approval prompt.
MANIFEST=http://localhost:8787/.well-known/stellar-agent-services.json
npx stellar-pay services $MANIFEST --dev
npx stellar-pay pay $MANIFEST text-stats '{"text":"Hello agents."}' --dev
```

Job Recovery: start the provider with `DRILL_LOSE_RESPONSE=1 REPORT_DELAY_SECONDS=8`, pay `delayed-report`,
then run the `stellar-pay recover <job-id> --dev` command it prints. `stellar-pay jobs` and
`stellar-pay journal verify` show the journal.

## Not done in the PoC

- `minVerificationScore` and `stellar.minProviderLevel` are stored but not enforced.
- The wallet secret is a plain file (mode 600). Testnet only.
- No MCP server yet.
- Only the built-in signer and method. Adapters for other wallets come later, each in its own package.


<!-- ===== apps/wallet/README.md ===== -->

# Agent Wallet (web approval page)

The page where a person sees the exact payment and approves it before anything is paid: the "web app" surface
of the payment client ([docs/payment-client.md](../../docs/payment-client.md)). It is a static page with no
backend. Every safety step runs in [`packages/payment-client`](../../packages/payment-client), in the browser.

**Status: minimal page (Week 1), Stellar testnet only.** It creates a test wallet, loads any Provider Standard v1
provider, builds the request form from the service's input schema, shows the approval screen, pays once, confirms
the transfer on chain and recovers lost jobs.

## Run it

```bash
npm install && npm run build                                  # builds the packages the page uses

# The sample provider (any public G... address with a USDC trustline receives the payments)
PAY_TO=G... node examples/paid-service/dist/server.js

# The page, on http://localhost:5173
npm run dev --workspace @stellar-agent-services/wallet
```

Then:

1. **Create test wallet.** This makes a key in the browser, gets test XLM from Friendbot and buys 5 test USDC on
   the testnet exchange.
2. **Use localhost:8787.** This loads the sample provider's manifest.
3. **Pick a service and review the payment.** The approval screen shows the price, the full payee address, when you
   are charged, and the challenge and spending-limit checks.
4. **Approve.** The page follows the payment and shows "Paid" only once the `transfer` on chain matches what you
   approved.

To show spending control, set the limit per payment to 0.01 and review `delayed-report` (0.02): the payment is
blocked before anything is signed.

For the Job Recovery demo, start the provider with `DRILL_LOSE_RESPONSE=1 REPORT_DELAY_SECONDS=10` and pay
`delayed-report`. The page says it can't tell whether the payment went through. **Recover job** then collects
the result with no second payment.

`npm run build --workspace @stellar-agent-services/wallet` writes the static page to `apps/wallet/dist`.

## How it keeps payments safe

- **Core.** The page never decides whether something is paid. It calls `quote()`, `pay()`, `decline()` and
  `recover()` on the core, and the core runs every check (docs/payment-client.md, "One payment, step by step").
- **Decline by default.** Closing the approval screen in any way declines: the Decline button, the close button,
  or Escape. The Decline button has the focus, so a stray Enter never pays.
- **Journal.** The journal and job tokens live in IndexedDB (`@stellar-agent-services/payment-client/browser`).
  - Writes use strict durability, so `sending` is on disk before the paid request goes out.
  - The page runs in one tab at a time (a Web Lock), so the journal has one writer.
  - If the journal can't be opened, nothing can be paid.
- **Key.** The test wallet's key is in this browser's site storage. That is fine for test money, never for real
  money: real wallets will plug in as signers (Stellar Wallets Kit, passkey accounts).
- **No outside code.** The page loads no third-party code, and a Content Security Policy blocks inline and outside
  scripts. `'unsafe-eval'` is allowed for Ajv, which compiles the manifest schema.
- **Local providers.** `http://localhost` providers are accepted only while the page itself runs on localhost, as
  with `stellar-pay --dev`.

## Files

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `src/lib/agent-wallet.svelte.ts` | The page's state and actions on top of the core; follows the journal for progress |
| `src/lib/schema-form.ts` | A service's `inputSchema` → form fields; anything else gets a JSON editor |
| `src/lib/jobs.ts` | Each job's state from the journal, for Recent payments |
| `src/lib/stellar.ts` | Test wallet balances and funding (Horizon, Friendbot, testnet exchange) |
| `src/lib/storage.ts` | The test wallet, the spending policy and service titles in site storage |
| `src/lib/format.ts` | Amounts, addresses and times for people |
| `src/components/` | `PayFlow` (provider, service, request), `ApprovalDialog`, `PaymentCard`, `WalletCard`, `LimitsCard`, `RecentPayments` |

## Not done yet

- Signers other than the test key: Stellar Wallets Kit (Freighter and others) and passkey accounts.
- Approval links from the MCP server, so an agent above its budget can send its human here.
- Verification badges on the approval screen (they need the verifier).
- Paying without a prompt below an amount (`autoApproveUpTo`). The page always asks.
- Precompiling the manifest validator, so the CSP can drop `'unsafe-eval'`.
- Hosting: any static host works, and it should send `frame-ancestors 'none'` as a header.


<!-- ===== docs/verification.md ===== -->

# Verification, receipts, badges and Validation Registry

How a provider is checked against [Provider Standard v1](provider-standard.md), and how the result becomes
evidence anyone can check: a verification receipt, badges, and a record in the Stellar 8004 Validation Registry.
The verifier is [`packages/verifier`](../packages/verifier).

## Contents

1. [Commands](#commands)
2. [Conformance levels](#conformance-levels)
3. [How the verifier works](#how-the-verifier-works)
4. [Checks](#checks)
5. [The test payer](#the-test-payer)
6. [Verification receipt](#verification-receipt)
7. [Badges](#badges)
8. [Stellar 8004 Validation Registry](#stellar-8004-validation-registry)
9. [Security considerations](#security-considerations)

## Commands

The packages are not on npm yet. After `npm install && npm run build` at the root of this repository:

```bash
alias verifier="node $PWD/packages/verifier/dist/cli/index.js"
```

| Command | What it does | Keys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `verifier check <manifest-url>` | Runs every check that needs no payment: C1, C2, C3, C6 and C7's burst. `--dev` also accepts a provider on `http://localhost`. | none |
| `verifier verify <manifest-url> --pay` | Runs every check, paying for C4, C5 and C7's paid part. With `--validator <G…> --out <dir>`, it writes the receipt. | test payer |
| `verifier badge <receipt.json>` | Writes the SVG badges the receipt earns. With `--request-hash`, also "8004 validated", once the record is on chain. | none |
| `verifier publish <receipt.json>` | Answers a validation request with the receipt (`validation_response`). | validator, through the Stellar CLI keychain |

A provider tests itself before going live:

```bash
verifier check http://localhost:8787/.well-known/stellar-agent-services.json --dev
```

A verifier answers a validation request, by the hash that the provider's `provider-kit request-validation` printed:

```bash
export VERIFIER_PAYER_SECRET=S...        # the dedicated testnet test payer (see below)
verifier verify https://api.example.com/.well-known/stellar-agent-services.json --pay \
  --validator $(stellar keys address verifier) --out evidence/receipts
# Publish evidence/receipts/<sha256>.json at an HTTPS URL, exactly as written, then:
verifier publish evidence/receipts/<sha256>.json --request-hash <hex> \
  --response-uri https://example.com/receipts/<sha256>.json --source verifier
verifier badge evidence/receipts/<sha256>.json --request-hash <hex>
```

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--service <name>`, `--input <json>` | The service to pay for and load, and its input. Default: the cheapest service with an example, and that example. |
| `--max-price <usdc>`, `--max-spend <usdc>` | The most the test payer pays for one job (default 0.10) and in one run (default 1.00). |
| `--allow-pubnet` | Pay a provider on pubnet, which is real money. |
| `--rpc <url>` | The Soroban RPC. Default: the public testnet RPC, or on pubnet the one the 8004 SDK uses. |
| `--json` | The report, or the receipt, as JSON on standard output; progress goes to standard error. |

**Exit codes:** `0` every check that ran passed, `1` a check or the command failed, `2` a usage error.

## Conformance levels

| Level | Name | Checks | Score | Badge |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | – | Level 1 not reached | 0 | none |
| 1 | Described | C1 manifest, C6 hygiene | 33 | Standard v1 |
| 2 | Payable | Level 1 + C3 challenge, C4 paid call | 67 | Payment verified |
| 3 | Recoverable | Level 2 + C5 recovery | 100 | Recovery verified |
| – | Registered | C2 identity, plus a Validation Registry record of the receipt | – | 8004 validated |
| – | Load-safe | C7 load | – | Load-safe |

A level counts only checks that **passed**. A skipped check earns nothing, so `verifier check`, which pays for
nothing, reaches level 1 at most.

## How the verifier works

- **From the standard, not from the kit.** The checks follow [provider-standard.md](provider-standard.md) and cite
  its rule ids. They don't reuse the Provider Kit, so a fault the kit shares with its providers can't pass unnoticed.
  The verifier's tests run them against the kit, as a provider that must pass, and against kit providers made to
  break one rule each.
- **MUST fails, SHOULD warns.** Each finding names a rule: an id such as `P4`, or a section such as `§5.5` for a
  requirement the standard states without an id. A broken MUST rule fails the check. An unmet SHOULD rule is a
  warning and never fails it. C7 is the exception: Load-safe certifies the SHOULD rules of §5.8, so they fail it.
- **Failed, or skipped.** A check fails only on what the provider did. When the verifier can't finish a check for
  its own reasons, such as an RPC outage or a provider that stayed busy, the check is skipped with a reason, and
  earns nothing.
- **A careful client.** The verifier sends what a conforming client sends: a fresh job id and token for each job
  [J1], the same request again after a `429` or `503` [Q8], polls no faster than `Retry-After` [Q9].
- **It pays only where a client would.** No payment unless C1 passed and the challenge matches the manifest [P7],
  within the verifier's own limits.
- **The chain decides.** A receipt is a claim [J16]. The verifier matches payments on chain by the auth-entry nonce
  it signed, so another job's payment can never pass as this one's. "Not charged" is proven too: once a payment's
  signature has expired, the chain must show no transfer for it.

Order of a run: C1, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6's probes, C7, then C6 over every exchange. The load test runs late so a
provider's rate limit can't turn away the other checks' requests.

## Checks

### C1 Manifest (§2)

The three steps of §2.4, and more.

| What | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| HTTPS (or loopback `http://` with `--dev`), `200`, `Content-Type: application/json` | M1 |
| No redirect, at most 256 KiB, I-JSON: UTF-8, no lone surrogates, no duplicate keys | M3 |
| `Cache-Control: max-age` of 300 s or less | M4 (warning) |
| The manifest URL has no user info | M6 |
| `standard` of another major version is rejected | M8 |
| The manifest JSON Schema, which also encodes M5, M6, M8, P1, S4 and S5; each error names its JSON Pointer | M9 |
| `checkManifestRules()`: same origin, unique names, schema sizes, examples, `payTo` checksum | M5, M7, S6, S9, P11 |
| Every `inputSchema` and `outputSchema` is a JSON Schema 2020-12 that compiles | §3.3 |
| `on-success` work expected to take at most half of `maxTimeoutSeconds` | S2 (warning) |
| No `if`/`then`/`else` or `patternProperties`, no `oneOf` or `allOf` at the root | S7 (warning) |
| Reverse-DNS extension keys | X1 (warning) |

Duplicate keys matter: `JSON.parse` keeps the last of two `payTo` members, while another parser may keep the
first, so two clients could show different payees.

C1 also decides what the run may do. The provider is **probed** only when the manifest passed the JSON Schema and
its `baseUrl` is on its own origin. It is **paid** only when C1 passed.

### C2 Identity (§7)

Reads only: the 8004 identity registry and the registration file.

| What | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| The agent exists | I2 |
| The registration file, from a `data:` or `https:` agent URI, lists `{ "name": "stellar-agent-services", "endpoint": <manifest URL>, "version": "1" }` | I1 |
| It also lists `{ "name": "web", "endpoint": <baseUrl> }` and sets `x402: true` | I1 (warning) |
| The agent's wallet, `get_agent_wallet(agentId)`, is the manifest's `payTo` | I3 |

Skipped without `provider.agentId`, in development mode, and when the registry or an `ipfs://` registration
can't be read. An `http://` agent URI fails: HTTPS is what proves the file's origin.

### C3 Challenge (§4)

With no payment, for every service the verifier has an input for: its first example that matches `inputSchema`,
the `--input` given for it, or an input built from the schema that validates against it.

| What | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| An input that fails `inputSchema` gets `400 invalid_input`, never a `402` | P8 |
| A valid input gets `402` with the x402 v2 `PAYMENT-REQUIRED` header | P3 |
| The challenge's one `accepts` entry equals the manifest's payment option plus the price | P4 |
| `resource.url` is the public create-job URL | P5 |
| The challenge carries the Bazaar extension | P6 (warning) |
| A `G…` `payTo` exists and holds an authorized USDC trustline | P2 |

### C4 Paid call (§4, §5)

The test payer pays for one job of the target service (`--service`, or the cheapest one with an example).

1. Unpaid create-job with a fresh job id and token: a `402` whose challenge matches the manifest. Otherwise
   nothing is signed [P7].
2. The payment is signed once and sent with the identical request. A busy answer is waited out with the same
   payment while it is valid [Q8], a `409` is followed with get-result [J7], and a lost response is recovered with
   get-result, never paid again.
3. Every job view is checked: the job id is the `Idempotency-Key` (§5.2), `charge` is the manifest's (§3.2),
   `charged` fits the state (§5.6), `200` once finished and otherwise `202` with `Retry-After`, plus `Location` on
   create-job [J8], output only when it may be shown [J14], and a receipt whose terms are the payment's (§5.7).
4. The job must succeed (§5.6), charged, with output that matches `outputSchema` [S1].
5. The receipt's transaction must have succeeded, carry the payment the verifier signed, and move exactly the
   price from the payer to `payTo` [J16]. The response that settled SHOULD carry `PAYMENT-RESPONSE` [P10].

### C5 Recovery (§5.3–§5.5, [job-recovery.md](job-recovery.md))

It recovers C4's job, as a client that lost the create-job response would.

| Request | Expected | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| create-job again: same id, token and input, no payment | `200` and the same job, no `402` | J5 |
| The same, with the same `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE` | the same job; the receipt still names the same transaction | J5, J16 |
| Same id, another input | `422 idempotency_key_reused` | J6 |
| Same id and input, another token | `422 idempotency_key_reused` | J6 |
| check-status and get-result with the token | `200` and the job, get-result with its output | J8, J15 |
| No token, a wrong token, an unknown job, on both | `404 job_not_found`, the same answer each time | J10 |

### C6 Hygiene

Two probes, then every exchange of the run.

| What | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| A body of `maxInputBytes` + 1 bytes is refused with `413 payload_too_large` | §5.4 |
| The job endpoints never redirect | §5.5 |
| Every error but `402` is `application/problem+json`, with a known `code` that goes with the HTTP status | E1 |
| `409` carries `Retry-After`; so do `429` and `503` | J7, §6 |
| No response contains a job token or a signed payment the verifier sent | E2 |
| No response contains a Stellar secret key | §10 |
| CORS on the manifest and the job endpoints, and a preflight that allows them | J17 (warning) |

### C7 Load (§5.8)

| What | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| 20 unpaid create-job requests at once: each answered within 30 s with `402`, or `429`/`503` with `Retry-After` | Q1 |
| With the test payer, once C4 passed: `capacity.concurrency` + 1 jobs paid at once (5 without `capacity`, at most 10) | |
| Each one accepted (`200`, or `202` with `queue` while queued) or refused with `429`/`503` and `Retry-After` | Q3, Q5 |
| Every accepted job finishes, and proves its own payment | Q4, J16 |
| A refused payment never lands: once its signature expired, the chain shows no transfer for it | Q3 |
| check-status and get-result keep answering at capacity | Q7 (warning) |

## The test payer

The paid checks are paid by a **dedicated** testnet account: create one for the verifier, fund it with XLM and
USDC, and keep nothing else in it. Its secret key is read from `VERIFIER_PAYER_SECRET` and stays in memory.

```bash
stellar keys generate verifier-payer --network testnet --fund
stellar tx new change-trust --source-account verifier-payer --network testnet \
  --line USDC:GBBD47IF6LWK7P7MDEVSCWR7DPUWV3NY3DTQEVFL4NAT4AQH3ZLLFLA5
# Testnet USDC: https://faucet.circle.com, or the testnet DEX (`stellar-pay wallet fund` does this for its own key).
export VERIFIER_PAYER_SECRET=$(stellar keys secret verifier-payer)   # `stellar keys show` in older versions
```

A full run against a service that costs 0.01 USDC signs for 0.06 USDC: one C4 job and five C7 jobs.

The verifier's own limits apply before anything is signed:
- one job costs at most `--max-price` (default 0.10 USDC), and a run signs for at most `--max-spend` (default 1.00
  USDC). A payment counts once signed, whether or not it settles;
- pubnet providers are paid only with `--allow-pubnet`;
- each signed payment is decoded before it is sent, and must move exactly the approved asset and amount, from the
  payer, to `payTo`.

## Verification receipt

The verifier issues one receipt per run (`VerificationReceipt` in
[packages/protocol](../packages/protocol/src/receipts.ts), JSON Schema
[verification-receipt.schema.json](../packages/protocol/schemas/verification-receipt.schema.json)). It is published as
RFC 8785 canonical JSON.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `standard` | `stellar-agent-services/provider@1` |
| `agentId` | The provider's Stellar 8004 agent id. Required to publish to the Validation Registry. |
| `network` | `stellar:testnet` or `stellar:pubnet` |
| `validator` | The verifier's `G…` address, which signs `validation_response` |
| `startedAt`, `checkedAt` | RFC 3339 |
| `level` | The conformance level reached, 0–3 (0: not even Described) |
| `score`, `scoreDirection` | 0, 33, 67 or 100 for levels 0–3; `higher-is-better`. `score` is also the on-chain `response`. |
| `manifest` | `{ url, sha256 }`, where `sha256` is the JCS hash of the parsed manifest. No `sha256` when the manifest could not be read as JSON. |
| `results[]` | One per check, in order C1–C7: `check`, `status` (`passed`, `failed`, `skipped`), `failedRules`, `warnings?`, `reason?` (why it was skipped), `findings?` (each rule, `fail` or `warn`, and what was observed), `evidence?` |
| `payment` | The C4 payment receipt, after the verifier confirmed it on chain |
| `tool` | The software that issued it: `{ name, version }` |

`standard`, `agentId`, `network`, `validator`, `checkedAt`, `score`, `scoreDirection` and `results` form the
envelope shared with Stellar ERC-8126 records ([erc-compatibility.md](erc-compatibility.md), T2).

**Rules beyond the JSON Schema:** `level` is the highest level whose checks all passed, and `score` is that level's.
`verifier badge` and `verifier publish` refuse a receipt that breaks either.

**One file, one hash.** The receipt is written to `<dir>/<sha256>.json`, holding exactly its canonical bytes with
no trailing newline. The name, the SHA-256 of the file and the on-chain `response_hash` are the same value, so
anyone can fetch the `response_uri`, hash it, and compare it with the chain. Upload the file as it is: reformatting
it changes the hash.

**What a receipt never holds:** secrets, job tokens, payment payloads, or text a provider chose. Messages quote a
provider's value only when it is a short plain token, such as an id or a status.

Receipts are issued only for providers served over HTTPS, never in development mode.

## Badges

SVG images derived **only** from a receipt, never from what a provider says about itself.

| Badge | Earned by |
| --- | --- |
| Standard v1 | Level 1 |
| Payment verified | Level 2 |
| Recovery verified | Level 3 |
| Load-safe | C7 passed |
| 8004 validated | C2 passed, and the Validation Registry anchors this receipt |

- **Each badge names the network**, "testnet" or "mainnet", so testnet evidence never passes for mainnet.
- **"8004 validated" needs the chain.** `verifier badge --request-hash <hex>` reads the request's record. The record
  must hold a response by the receipt's validator, for its agent, with its hash, its score and the tag
  `provider-standard-v1`.
- **The badge links back to its evidence.** Its description carries the receipt's SHA-256. Where a badge is shown,
  link it to the receipt.
- **Safe to embed anywhere.** The SVG is self-contained (no fonts, scripts or links), accessible (`role="img"` with a
  title), and the same receipt always gives the same bytes.

Files are written next to the receipt as `<sha256>.<badge>.svg`, for example `<sha256>.payment-verified.svg`.

## Stellar 8004 Validation Registry

The registry ([contract](https://github.com/trionlabs/stellar-8004/tree/main/contracts/validation-registry), testnet
`CC5USZRO26MOIAVNYTTJDS63C2OBBLREOAOET4CPF2EZWO3YFKLMO3SL`) keeps one record per request. Only the validator a
request names may answer it, and may update its answer later.

### 1. The provider's owner asks

```
validation_request(caller = owner, validator_address = <verifier G…>, agent_id, request_uri, request_hash)
```

The request document names what is to be verified (`ValidationRequest` in
[packages/protocol](../packages/protocol/src/validation-request.ts), JSON Schema
[validation-request.schema.json](../packages/protocol/schemas/validation-request.schema.json)):

```json
{
  "standard": "stellar-agent-services/provider@1",
  "type": "validation-request",
  "agentId": 42,
  "network": "stellar:testnet",
  "manifest": { "url": "https://api.example.com/.well-known/stellar-agent-services.json" },
  "validator": "GBZSBASBFMV5RGKPRIPCB5QQVAJ35IXKMTF2A2766MOA4ZHQ7MLSIPXU",
  "requestedAt": "2026-10-26T10:00:00Z"
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `standard`, `type` | `stellar-agent-services/provider@1`, `validation-request` |
| `agentId`, `network` | The provider's Stellar 8004 agent id, and `stellar:testnet` or `stellar:pubnet` |
| `manifest` | `{ url }`: the HTTPS manifest URL the agent's registration names [I1] |
| `validator` | The verifier's `G…` address: the only account that may answer |
| `requestedAt` | RFC 3339 |

- **One document, one hash.** `request_hash` is the SHA-256 of the document's RFC 8785 canonical JSON, the
  `contentHash` mode of `generateRequestNonce`. `request_uri` holds exactly those bytes: a
  `data:application/json;base64,` URI, or an HTTPS URL serving them. Anyone can hash what the URI holds and compare it
  with the chain. [validation-requests.json](../packages/protocol/test-vectors/validation-requests.json) pins both.
- **Every request is new.** `requestedAt` makes each document unique, and the registry refuses a hash it already has.
- **Who may ask.** The registry takes a request only from the agent's owner, the address approved for the agent, or an
  operator of the owner's.
- **Never the provider itself.** The validator is not the agent's owner or its wallet. The registry would accept such a
  request, but its answer would prove nothing.
- **Ready to verify.** The provider is served over HTTPS and its registration passes [I1]–[I3]. Otherwise C2 fails, and
  the answer can never earn "8004 validated".

`provider-kit request-validation` checks all of this before anything is signed, puts the document on chain as a
`data:` URI, signs through the Stellar CLI keychain and reads the registry back:

```bash
provider-kit request-validation --config provider.config.json --validator <verifier G…> --source owner --dry-run
provider-kit request-validation --config provider.config.json --validator <verifier G…> --source owner --out request.json
```

It prints the request hash, which the provider sends the verifier with its manifest URL. `--manifest <url>` instead of
`--config` works for any provider, library or native. Without the kit, the owner sends the same request with the
Stellar CLI:

```bash
stellar contract invoke --id CC5USZRO26MOIAVNYTTJDS63C2OBBLREOAOET4CPF2EZWO3YFKLMO3SL --source-account owner \
  --network testnet -- validation_request --caller $(stellar keys address owner) \
  --validator_address <verifier G…> --agent_id 42 --request_uri <uri> --request_hash <hex>
```

### 2. The verifier answers

```
validation_response(caller = validator, request_hash, response = score, response_uri = receipt URL,
                    response_hash = sha256(receipt), tag = "provider-standard-v1")
```

`verifier publish` checks everything before the Stellar CLI signs, and refuses when anything is off:
- the receipt is valid, and recent: checked within `--max-age` hours, default 24;
- the request exists, names this validator and the receipt's agent, on the receipt's network;
- `response_uri` is HTTPS and serves exactly the receipt's bytes;
- the `--source` key is the receipt's validator.

The validator key stays in the Stellar CLI keychain; the verifier never reads it. After sending, `publish` reads the
record back to confirm it.

### 3. Anyone reads it

`get_validation_status(request_hash)` returns the validator, agent, score, `response_hash` and tag;
`get_agent_validations_paginated(agent_id)` lists an agent's requests. Fetch the `response_uri`, check its SHA-256
against `response_hash`, and read the receipt. `get_summary(agent_id, validators, "provider-standard-v1")` averages
this standard's records without mixing in other kinds ([erc-compatibility.md](erc-compatibility.md), T2).

## Security considerations

- **Keys.** The test payer holds testnet USDC only, within the verifier's limits. The validator key signs through
  the Stellar CLI keychain and never enters the verifier. Neither is shared with providers, discovery or the payment
  client.
- **The provider is untrusted.** Every request has a deadline and a size limit on its answer, and no redirect is
  followed. Once the manifest names its origin, the verifier sends requests to that origin only, so a manifest can't
  point the load test at someone else's server.
- **Provider schemas are untrusted.** Each compiles in its own Ajv instance, after a check against the JSON Schema
  2020-12 meta-schema; nothing remote is fetched [S5]. A provider can still slow its own run down with a costly
  regular expression in a `pattern`. A verifier run as a shared service should run each verification in its own
  process with a time limit.
- **Address checks.** The verifier does not resolve host names to refuse private addresses. A verifier run as a
  shared service should run where it can reach only the public internet.
- **No secrets in evidence.** Job tokens and signed payments are kept in memory to check that no response echoes
  them [E2], and never written to a receipt or a report.


<!-- ===== packages/verifier/README.md ===== -->

# @stellar-agent-services/verifier

Checks a provider against [Provider Standard v1](../../docs/provider-standard.md) and turns the result into evidence
anyone can check:

1. **Checks C1–C7:** manifest, identity, payment challenge, paid call, recovery, hygiene and load. Each finding
   cites a rule of the standard.
2. **Verification receipt:** RFC 8785 canonical JSON, stored under its own SHA-256.
3. **Badges:** SVGs drawn only from a receipt.
4. **Validation Registry:** `validation_response` anchors the receipt's hash in the Stellar 8004 Validation
   Registry.

The full description, with every check and rule, is [docs/verification.md](../../docs/verification.md).

## Use

```bash
# After npm install && npm run build at the repository root:
alias verifier="node $PWD/packages/verifier/dist/cli/index.js"

# A provider testing itself, with no payment and no key:
verifier check http://localhost:8787/.well-known/stellar-agent-services.json --dev

# A verifier: every check, paid by a dedicated testnet account, and a receipt.
VERIFIER_PAYER_SECRET=S... verifier verify https://api.example.com/.well-known/stellar-agent-services.json \
  --pay --validator G... --out evidence/receipts
verifier publish evidence/receipts/<sha256>.json --request-hash <hex> --response-uri <https url> --source verifier
verifier badge evidence/receipts/<sha256>.json --request-hash <hex>
```

```
Provider Standard v1 check: http://localhost:8787/.well-known/stellar-agent-services.json
  ✓ C1 Manifest
  - C2 Identity: skipped, development mode: a loopback provider can't be registered
  ✓ C3 Challenge
  - C4 Paid call: skipped, no test payer: run verifier verify --pay
  - C5 Recovery: skipped, no test payer: run verifier verify --pay
  ✓ C6 Hygiene
  ✓ C7 Load

Level 1 (Described): score 33 of 100.
Load (C7) passed: Load-safe.
Every check that ran passed.
```

Exit codes: `0` every check that ran passed, `1` a check or the command failed, `2` a usage error. `--json` prints
the report, or the receipt, on standard output.

As a library:

```ts
import { issueReceipt, localKeyPayer, verifyProvider, writeReceipt } from "@stellar-agent-services/verifier";

const report = await verifyProvider({ manifestUrl, payer: localKeyPayer(process.env.VERIFIER_PAYER_SECRET!) });
const receipt = issueReceipt(report, { validator: "G..." });
const { path, sha256 } = await writeReceipt(receipt, "evidence/receipts");
```

## Keys

| Key | Used for | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Test payer | C4, C5 and C7's paid part | `VERIFIER_PAYER_SECRET`: a dedicated testnet account holding a little USDC |
| Validator | `validation_response` | The Stellar CLI keychain. `verifier publish --source <key>` signs through it; the verifier never sees it. |

The test payer pays only a provider whose manifest passed C1 and whose challenge matches it, at most 0.10 USDC for
a job and 1.00 USDC in a run unless told otherwise, and never on pubnet without `--allow-pubnet`.

## Layout

| Path | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `src/verify.ts` | `verifyProvider()`: runs the checks, in order, and returns the report |
| `src/checks/` | One module per check, C1–C7 |
| `src/jobs.ts` | The job endpoints, called as a careful client calls them, and the job view checks (§5.5–§5.7) |
| `src/http.ts` | The HTTP client for an untrusted provider: no redirects, deadlines, size limits, one origin |
| `src/payments.ts` | The test payer and its limits |
| `src/chain.ts` | Soroban RPC reads: the trustline, and the proofs that a payment did or did not settle |
| `src/registry.ts` | Stellar 8004 reads: identity and validation records |
| `src/receipt.ts`, `src/badges.ts`, `src/publish.ts` | Receipts, badges, and the Validation Registry response |
| `src/cli/` | The `verifier` command |

## Tests

The tests run every check against the real Provider Kit in-process, with a facilitator that settles onto a fake
Soroban chain and a test payer that signs real payments offline. A conforming provider must pass every check; for
each rule, a provider made to break it must fail with that rule's id.


<!-- ===== docs/job-recovery.md ===== -->

# Job Recovery

The normative rules are in [provider-standard.md §5](provider-standard.md#5-jobs). This document explains how they
fit together, how the Provider Kit and the payment client implement them, and how the recovery demo is run.
Short version: [recovery/README.md](recovery/README.md). For AI coding agents:
[recovery/README-AI.md](recovery/README-AI.md).

**Goal:** if a connection drops after payment, the user collects the same job's result without paying again.
Nobody is charged twice for one job. A payment whose outcome is unknown is decided from the chain, never by
charging again.

## Operations

| Operation | Request | Auth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| create-job | `POST {baseUrl}/services/{name}/jobs` | x402 payment |
| check-status | `GET {baseUrl}/jobs/{jobId}` | `Job-Token` |
| get-result | `GET {baseUrl}/jobs/{jobId}/result` | `Job-Token` |

All three answer with the same job view (§5.5): `200` once the job is `succeeded` or `failed`, otherwise `202`
with `Retry-After`, plus `Location` on create-job. The paths are fixed under `baseUrl`, so a client that kept
`baseUrl`, the job id and the token can always reach the job, even if it lost every response. check-status and
get-result never take a payment and never charge [J11].

## Job identity and binding

1. Before the first request, the client generates the job id (a lowercase UUID, sent as `Idempotency-Key`) and a
   `Job-Token` (32 random bytes), and saves both. The payment client writes them to its journal and secret store
   before it calls create-job.
2. The provider binds the job id, permanently [J4], to:
   - the binding hash, `sha256(JCS({ service, input }))`;
   - `sha256(Job-Token)`. The token itself is never stored [J3].
3. Repeated requests get these answers:

| Request | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| create-job with the same id, binding and token | The existing job. No new `402`, and a payment the request carries is not settled [J5]. |
| create-job with the same id and other input or another token | `422 idempotency_key_reused` [J6] |
| create-job, check-status or get-result while the payment is still being claimed or settled | `409 request_in_progress` with `Retry-After` [J7] |
| check-status or get-result with a wrong token, or for an unknown or expired job | `404 job_not_found`, which never says whether the job exists [J10] |

A client that sends neither header (any plain x402 client) gets a provider-generated id and token in the
create-job response [J2]. It can pay, but if that response is lost, so is the job.

## States

```
(new)              → queued | running | payment_uncertain | failed
queued             → running
running            → succeeded | failed | payment_uncertain    (payment_uncertain: on-success only)
payment_uncertain  → queued | succeeded | failed               (decided from on-chain data)
```

| `status` | `charged` |
| --- | --- |
| `queued`, `running` | `true` for `upfront`, `false` for `on-success` |
| `succeeded` | `true` |
| `failed` | `true` for `upfront` unless `error.code` is `payment_failed`; `false` for `on-success` |
| `payment_uncertain` | `"unknown"`. The output is withheld [J14]. |

`succeeded` and `failed` are final [J12]. Finished jobs stay retrievable for `jobs.retentionSeconds` [J15]. The
kit also has an internal `pending` state: an `upfront` job whose settlement has not answered yet. Requests for it
get `409`.

## When the user is charged

| `charge` | Order | If the work fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `on-success` | verify → work → settle | Not charged |
| `upfront` (default) | verify → settle → work | Charged. v1 has no refunds. |

A signed Stellar payment is valid up to an **expiration ledger**, about `maxTimeoutSeconds` (30–300) after
signing [S2]. `on-success` therefore suits work well inside that window, and the kit refuses an `on-success`
service whose `expectedDurationSeconds` is more than half of `maxTimeoutSeconds`.

The kit times each `on-success` job by its payment's expiration ledger, using the ledger clock (see
[Reconciliation](#reconciliation)). It stops 10 s before that ledger closes, to leave time to settle. A job that
can't finish in time fails with `timeout` and is not charged, even when the client sent its payment long after
signing [Q8]. Long or expensive work uses `upfront`: it is paid before it starts, and its place in the queue
survives restarts [Q4].

## Why nobody pays twice

There are five independent guards, and each one alone stops a second charge.

1. **The client fixes the identity before paying.** The job id, token and binding are journaled before the first
   request, and `sending` is journaled and flushed before the paid request goes out. From then on the client
   never signs for that job again: `pay()` refuses, and `recover()` only reads.
2. **The provider binds the job.** One job id has one binding and one token, forever [J4]. A repeated create-job
   returns the same job and never settles the payment it carries [J5].
3. **The provider binds the payment.** The payment fingerprint is `sha256(JCS({ network, payer, nonce }))`, taken
   from the payer's signed Soroban auth entry. Soroban accepts an (address, nonce) pair once, and the store
   refuses a second job for one fingerprint. A signed payment buys at most one job, however it is re-wrapped
   [P9].
4. **Uncertain means don't pay.** When settlement times out, errors or answers something unexpected, the job
   becomes `payment_uncertain` and is never settled again [J13]. Only a facilitator answer saying the
   transaction was never submitted counts as failed.
5. **Recovery never re-sends `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE`.** It calls check-status and get-result only.

The client checks the receipt as well. Before it shows "paid", it confirms on chain that the transaction moved
the approved amount from the payer to `payTo`, and it accepts one transaction as proof for one job only [J16].

## Reconciliation

A `payment_uncertain` job is decided from on-chain data [J13]. In the kit, `jobs/reconcile.ts` applies the
decision and `payments/onchain.ts` does the lookup.

**What identifies the payment.** The amount and recipient can't: the same payer may pay the same provider the
same price for several jobs. Instead the kit looks for the successful transaction that carries the payer's signed
auth entry **with the job's nonce**, which the provider stored when it claimed the job. Soroban accepts that pair
once, so that transaction is the job's payment, and no other transaction can be.

**Where it looks.**

1. The transaction hash the facilitator named, if there is one.
2. Otherwise, or if that transaction failed (a facilitator may retry), the USDC `transfer` events from the payer
   in every ledger the payment could have landed in: the 320 ledgers up to its expiration ledger. Those cover
   every possible ledger, because the provider and the facilitator both refuse a signature that expires more than
   `maxTimeoutSeconds` (at most 300) of ledgers after verification, and a ledger takes at least a second.

**What it decides.**

| Found | Decision | The job becomes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A successful transaction that carries the payment, with its `transfer` event | settled | `upfront`: `queued` with the receipt, and a worker runs it. `on-success`: `succeeded` with the receipt; the output was stored before settling. |
| Nothing, after the expiration ledger closed and every ledger of the window was searched | not settled | `failed` with `payment_failed`, `charged: false` |
| Anything less | undecided | Stays `payment_uncertain` |

"Undecided" covers a payment that can still land (its expiration ledger hasn't closed), a window older than the
RPC's history, an RPC error, and a transaction that used the payment but shows no matching transfer. The job
waits. Nothing is decided from a guess.

**Who runs it.**

- The provider itself, after every recovery sweep (every 30 s), when it has a Soroban RPC: `rpc` in
  `createProvider()`, or `rpcUrl` in a gateway config. Testnet defaults to the public RPC. Mainnet has no public
  RPC, so set your own.
- The operator, with `provider-kit reconcile`:

```bash
provider-kit reconcile --config provider.config.json --dry-run   # what would change
provider-kit reconcile --config provider.config.json             # decide
provider-kit reconcile --store ./jobs.sqlite --network testnet   # a library provider's store
```

The command reads the chain and writes only the job store. It is safe to run next to a running provider, and it
exits 1 while any job is still undecided. `--rpc <url>` uses another RPC, such as one that keeps more history.

Every update is compare-and-set from `payment_uncertain`. A late facilitator answer, another process or a second
run can't overturn a decision, and they all read the same chain.

**The ledger clock.** The same RPC gives the kit a clock on ledgers (`payments/chain.ts`): the latest ledger, its
close time, and the average ledger duration over the last 100 ledgers. The clock is used to:

- time `on-success` jobs (see [When the user is charged](#when-the-user-is-charged));
- let the recovery sweep fail an `on-success` job, uncharged, as soon as its payment's expiration ledger has
  passed;
- let create-job refuse a payment that expires too far out.

When the RPC is slow or down, all three fall back to the claim time plus `maxTimeoutSeconds`, and payments keep
working.

## Clients

The payment client (`packages/payment-client`) recovers like this:

- `pay()` journals `sending` before it sends the paid request. If that request fails in transit, the journal
  marks the job `uncertain`, and `PaymentUncertainError` says to recover the job, never to pay again.
- A `409 request_in_progress` means the provider holds the payment and is still settling it. The client polls
  get-result at the provider's `Retry-After` until it has a job view, for up to `followSeconds`. If settlement
  takes longer, it hands the job back for `recover()`.
- `recover(jobId)` (`stellar-pay recover <job-id>`) reads the job id and token from the journal and calls
  get-result. It never signs.
- A `payment_uncertain` job comes back at once. Only the provider's reconciliation decides it, so polling doesn't
  help; recover the job again later.

## Response-loss drill

The SOW recovery demo needs a response lost after a real payment. The kit has a test-only switch for this:
`loseCreateJobResponse: true`, or `DRILL_LOSE_RESPONSE=1` in the example provider. With it, the provider verifies
the payment, claims the job, settles and stores the result, then drops the create-job response. It is off by
default. Never enable it in production.

To run the demo on testnet:

```bash
# 1. The example provider, with the drill on (after npm install && npm run build at the root)
cd examples/paid-service
DRILL_LOSE_RESPONSE=1 PAY_TO=G... npm start

# 2. Pay for a job. The response is lost after the payment.
MANIFEST=http://localhost:8787/.well-known/stellar-agent-services.json
npx stellar-pay pay $MANIFEST text-stats '{"text":"lost and found"}' --dev
#    ⚠ ... The payment may have gone through: recover job <job-id>, do not pay again.

# 3. Collect the result without paying
npx stellar-pay recover <job-id> --dev
```

The evidence is the recovered result, plus the payer's account on stellar.expert showing exactly one USDC
transfer for the job.


<!-- ===== docs/recovery/README-AI.md ===== -->

# Job Recovery: implementation reference for AI coding agents

Use this file to change, extend, review or debug Job Recovery in this repository: the provider's reconciliation
of `payment_uncertain` jobs, the ledger clock, and the payment client's recovery paths.

- **Normative source:** [provider-standard.md §5](../provider-standard.md#5-jobs). If this file and the spec
  disagree, the spec wins. Cite rules by id (`[J13]`). v1 is frozen: additions must be optional fields or SHOULD
  rules.
- **Explanatory doc:** [job-recovery.md](../job-recovery.md). **Human summary:** [README.md](README.md).
- **State:** implemented and tested offline (`npm test`). Checked read-only against the public testnet
  RPC. Not yet done: the recorded testnet demo (one interrupted job recovered with exactly one on-chain transfer).

## 0. Invariants: never break these

1. **Never charge twice.** A `payment_uncertain` job is never settled again [J13]. Recovery never re-sends
   `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE`; check-status and get-result never charge [J11].
2. **Fail closed on money.** `not_settled` needs proof of absence (§4.3). Any doubt is `undecided`, and the job
   stays `payment_uncertain`. Never report a paid job as unpaid.
3. **Identify a payment by `(payer, nonce)`, never by amount and recipient.** One payer may pay one provider the
   same price for many jobs. Soroban accepts an `(address, nonce)` pair once, so that pair identifies exactly one
   payment.
4. **Every reconciliation write is compare-and-set from `payment_uncertain`.** A late facilitator answer,
   another process or a second run must not overturn a decision.
5. **The provider holds no secret key.** Chain access is read-only Soroban RPC.
6. **Tests never touch the network.** Test providers pass `rpc: false` or a fake `ChainReader`
   (`packages/provider-kit/test/support/chain.ts`).

## 1. File map

| File | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `packages/protocol/src/networks.ts` | `SOROBAN_RPC_URL`: testnet `https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org`, pubnet `undefined` (no public SDF RPC) |
| `packages/provider-kit/src/payments/chain.ts` | `ChainReader` type, `rpcChain()`, `LedgerClock`, `ledgerClock()` |
| `packages/provider-kit/src/payments/onchain.ts` | `findPayment()`, `PaymentLookup`, `PaymentSearch`, `SEARCH_WINDOW_LEDGERS`, `EXPIRATION_TOLERANCE_LEDGERS` |
| `packages/provider-kit/src/jobs/reconcile.ts` | `reconcile()`: lists `payment_uncertain` jobs, calls `findPayment`, applies decisions |
| `packages/provider-kit/src/jobs/recovery.ts` | `sweep()`: now also fails on-success jobs by expiration ledger (`SweepOptions.clock`) |
| `packages/provider-kit/src/jobs/runner.ts` | `paymentDeadline()`: on-success deadline from the expiration ledger; `PaidRun.clock` |
| `packages/provider-kit/src/http/router.ts` | Step 7: refuses a signature that expires too far out; `RouterContext.clock` |
| `packages/provider-kit/src/provider.ts` | `ProviderConfig.rpc`; builds chain and clock; background `reconcileJobs()` after each sweep |
| `packages/provider-kit/src/payments/payload-checks.ts` | `addressCredentials()` is now exported (shared with `onchain.ts`) |
| `packages/provider-kit/src/gateway/config.ts`, `schemas/gateway-config.schema.json` | `rpcUrl` (allows `env:NAME`) maps to `ProviderConfig.rpc` |
| `packages/provider-kit/src/cli/reconcile.ts`, `cli/main.ts`, `cli/shared.ts` | `provider-kit reconcile` command; new flags `--store`, `--rpc` |
| `packages/payment-client/src/client.ts` | 409 handling: `isInProgress()`, `whileSettling()`, changes in `payOnce`, `follow`, `getResult`, `recover` |
| `packages/payment-client/src/onchain.ts` | Uses `SOROBAN_RPC_URL` from protocol (its local copy was removed) |
| `examples/paid-service/src/server.ts`, `.env.example` | Optional `SOROBAN_RPC_URL` passed as `rpc` |

## 2. Spec mapping

| Rule | Where it is enforced |
| --- | --- |
| [J5] same id + binding + token returns the existing job, no settle | `router.ts` `existingJob()` (existing code) |
| [J7] `409 request_in_progress` while claimed or settled | Provider: `router.ts`, for internal status `pending`. Client: `isInProgress()` means "ask again later". |
| [J11] check-status and get-result never charge | `router.ts` `handleGetJob()`; client `recover()` only calls get-result |
| [J12] final states never change | Store `update()` refuses final `from`; reconcile is compare-and-set from `payment_uncertain` |
| [J13] uncertain decided on chain, never re-charged | `jobs/reconcile.ts` + `payments/onchain.ts` |
| [J14] output withheld while uncertain | Existing router logic; reconcile keeps the stored output for on-success |
| [J16] receipt confirmed on chain | Client `confirm()` (existing); reconcile also requires a matching `transfer` event |
| [S2] payment expires about `maxTimeoutSeconds` after signing | `runner.ts` `paymentDeadline()`, `recovery.ts` sweep, router step-7 check |
| [P9] one signed payment buys at most one job | Fingerprint `sha256(JCS({network, payer, nonce}))` (existing) |
| [Q8], [Q9] retries and polling pace | Client follows `Retry-After` for 409, 429 and 503 |

## 3. Data the provider stores (existing, relied on)

`StoredJob.claim: PaymentClaim` = `{ fingerprint, payer, nonce, expirationLedger }`, written at claim time from
`checkPayment()`. `nonce` is the payer auth entry's `credentials.nonce().toString()` (decimal int64).
`expirationLedger` is `signatureExpirationLedger`, the last ledger at which the signature is valid.

`StoredJob.settlement?: { reason, transaction? }` is set when the job became `payment_uncertain`. `transaction`
is the hash the facilitator named, if any.

Internal status `pending`: an upfront job claimed, with settlement in flight. It has no job view; requests get 409.

## 4. Reconciliation algorithm

### 4.1 `reconcile(store, options): Promise<Reconciled[]>` (`jobs/reconcile.ts`)

```
options: PaymentSearch & { dryRun?: boolean; limit?: number }   // limit default 500 (CLI uses 1000)
PaymentSearch: { chain: ChainReader; network: StellarNetwork; asset: string }   // asset = manifest USDC SAC

1. jobs = store.list({ statuses: ["payment_uncertain"], createdBefore: now + 1 s, limit })   // oldest first
2. if none: return []                                       // no RPC call at all
3. health = chain.getHealth()                               // once per run
   on error: every job → undecided("the chain could not be read: …"), no writes
4. for each job:
     if job.claim.expirationLedger < health.oldestLedger:
         undecided("older than the RPC's history")         // no RPC call, so a backlog costs nothing
     else lookup = findPayment(job.claim, job.settlement?.transaction, options, health)
     apply(lookup)                                          // §4.4
```

`Reconciled = { jobId, service, outcome: "settled" | "not_settled" | "undecided", status, transaction?, reason? }`.
`status` is the status afterwards (in a dry run, the status it would get).

### 4.2 `findPayment(claim, known, search, health?)` (`payments/onchain.ts`)

```
check(hash): getTransaction(hash) → paymentIn(...)          // each hash checked once (Set)

1. if known: r = check(known); if r: return r               // settled or undecided; a FAILED tx falls through
2. range = health ?? getHealth()
   end   = claim.expirationLedger
   from  = max(1, end - SEARCH_WINDOW_LEDGERS)               // 320
   start = max(from, range.oldestLedger)
   latest = range.latestLedger
3. if start <= min(end, latest):
     filters = [{ type: "contract", contractIds: [asset],
                  topics: [[sym("transfer"), addr(payer), "*", "*"],     // SAC: 4 topics
                           [sym("transfer"), addr(payer), "*"]] }]       // other SEP-41 tokens: 3 topics
     request = { filters, startLedger: start, endLedger: min(end, latest) + 1, limit: 100 }   // endLedger is exclusive
     loop pages (max 10, else undecided "more transfers than reconciliation searches"):
       response = getEvents(request); latest = min(latest, response.latestLedger)
       for event: if event.ledger > end: stop
                  r = check(event.txHash); if r: return r
       if stopped, or events < 100: break
       request = { filters, cursor: response.cursor, limit: 100 }   // cursor mode can't take endLedger
4. if latest <= end:  undecided("the payment can still land until ledger {end} closes")
5. if start > from:   undecided("ledgers {from}–{start-1} are older than the RPC's history")
6. return not_settled("no transaction used the payment before it expired at ledger {end}")
Any exception: undecided("the chain could not be read: …")
```

`latest` is the **minimum** of every reported latest ledger: several RPC nodes behind one URL may lag
differently, and coverage is only as far as the least advanced node.

**Do not filter on `event.inSuccessfulContractCall`.** Current RPCs leave this deprecated field unset
(`undefined`). An earlier version of this code skipped every real event because of it; the live testnet check
caught it. The transaction's own `SUCCESS` status decides.

### 4.3 `paymentIn(tx, hash, claim, search)`: is this transaction the payment?

```
tx.status !== SUCCESS                                → undefined (not the payment; keep looking)
signedTransfer(tx.envelopeXdr, claim, asset):
  operations: fee-bump → innerTx().v1().tx().operations(); v1 → v1().tx(); else v0().tx()
  for each invokeHostFunction op, for each auth entry:
    credentials = addressCredentials(entry.credentials())     // address or addressV2
    skip unless address == claim.payer && nonce == claim.nonce
    rootInvocation must be contractFn on `asset`, function "transfer", args [from, to, amount],
      with from == payer, to a string and amount a bigint            → { to, amount }
    anything else with this (payer, nonce): undefined (the nonce was spent elsewhere, not this payment)
no matching entry                                    → undefined
transfersFrom(tx.events.contractEventsXdr.flat(), asset, payer) has no event with the same to and amount
                                                     → undecided("used the payment, but … no transfer …")
otherwise → settled, receipt = { network, asset, amount, payTo: to, payer, transaction: hash,
                                 settledAt: ISO(tx.createdAt * 1000) }
```

The transfer event data is an `i128`, or a map with `amount` for a muxed payee (CAP-67). Both are handled.

### 4.4 Applying a decision

| Lookup | `charge` | Patch, compare-and-set from `payment_uncertain` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `settled` | `upfront` | `{ status: "queued", payment: receipt }`. The store enqueues it; the provider wakes the lane and a worker leases it. `input` is still stored (it's dropped only at a final status). |
| `settled` | `on-success` | `{ status: "succeeded", payment: receipt }`. The output was stored before settling. If `output` is missing (a broken store), report `undecided`: never report a paid job as unpaid. |
| `not_settled` | any | `{ status: "failed", error: jobError("payment_failed", …) }`. `chargedFor()` gives `false`. |
| `undecided` | any | No write. |

When the compare-and-set misses (the job changed meanwhile), the reported status is re-read from the store, and
the earlier decision stands.

### 4.5 Why the 320-ledger window is sound

- The x402 facilitator refuses `signatureExpirationLedger > currentLedger + ceil(maxTimeout / estLedgerSecs) + 2`
  at verify.
- The provider adds its own check at router step 7, only when the clock answers:
  `expirationLedger > latest + maxTimeoutSeconds + EXPIRATION_TOLERANCE_LEDGERS (10)` → 402 with
  `invalid_exact_stellar_payload_signature_expiration_too_far`, before the facilitator sees the payment. This
  counts a ledger as at least 1 s.
- `maxTimeoutSeconds` is at most 300 (§4.1), so `E ≤ claimLedger + 310`, so `E − 320 ≤ claimLedger − 10`.
- A payment lands after verification. Before verification, a used nonce would fail the facilitator's
  simulation, and the job would never be claimed.
- If the clock is down at claim time, the window relies on the facilitator's check alone.

## 5. Ledger clock (`payments/chain.ts`)

```ts
interface LedgerClock { latest(): Promise<number>; closesAt(ledger: number): Promise<number /* epoch ms */> }
ledgerClock(chain: Pick<ChainReader, "getLatestLedger" | "getLedgers">): LedgerClock
```

- **A reading:** `getLatestLedger()`, then `getLedgers({ startLedger: latest - 100, pagination: { limit: 1 } })`.
  `ledgerMs = (latestLedgerCloseTime - sample.ledgerCloseTime) * 1000 / (latestLedger - sample.sequence)`, kept
  only within [1000, 60000]. Default 5000. If `getLedgers` fails, the latest ledger and the default duration
  serve. If there is no usable close time, `Date.now()` stands in.
- `closesAt(L) = closedAt + (L - sequence) * ledgerMs`. `latest()` is the reading's real sequence, never
  extrapolated.
- **Cache 5 s, timeout 3 s per reading.** A failed reading rejects until the next one is due, and warns once per
  failure streak. A slow RPC never holds a request or job for more than 3 s.
- **Users:**
  - `runner.ts` `paymentDeadline(job, run) = min(createdAt + max(1, maxTimeout − 10) s, closesAt(E) − 10 s)`.
    If the clock fails, the claim-time deadline alone applies.
  - `recovery.ts` `sweep()`: an on-success job, `queued` or `running`, with no `settlingSince`, fails `timeout`
    uncharged when `createdAt < now − (maxTimeout + 60) s` **or** `clock.latest() > claim.expirationLedger`.
